name: Germany
description: Germany attracts expats with its robust economy, high quality of life, and efficient public services. It offers a stable environment with excellent healthcare and education systems, making it a desirable destination for both singles and families.
longdescription:
Expat life in Germany is characterized by a high standard of living, strong social security, and a well-developed infrastructure. The country boasts a universal, multi-payer healthcare system often recognized as one of the best globally. Its economy, the largest in the European Union, provides numerous job opportunities, particularly in engineering, IT, sales, and marketing. Germany values a healthy work-life balance, with many employees enjoying 20-30 days of annual leave and a focus on efficient working hours.

Culturally, Germany is known for its orderliness and respect for rules. While Germans can be perceived as reserved, building social networks is possible through local groups and activities. Expats may initially face challenges with bureaucracy and the language barrier, as fluency in German is often crucial for full integration and professional advancement. Despite a modern infrastructure, digitalization in some areas like high-speed internet availability and cashless payment options can sometimes lag. The cost of living is generally affordable compared to other Western European countries, though major cities like Munich and Frankfurt are more expensive.

visas.name: Germany EU Blue Card (Qualified)
visas.description: The Germany EU Blue Card is a residence permit for highly qualified non-EU/EEA nationals who wish to live and work in Germany. It requires a recognized university degree (or, in specific cases like IT specialists, substantial professional experience) and a binding job offer in Germany that meets a specified minimum annual gross salary. This visa provides a streamlined path to permanent residency and facilitates family reunification.
benefits: Faster path to permanent residency (21-33 months).
Easier family reunification, allowing spouses to work without German language requirements.
EU-wide mobility rights after 12-18 months.
Visa-free travel within the Schengen Area for up to 90 days in any 180-day period.
Access to social security benefits (health insurance, pension, unemployment insurance).
visas.path_to_residency_description: EU Blue Card holders can obtain a permanent residence permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) after 21 months with B1 level German language skills, or after 33 months with A1 level German language skills, provided they have made pension contributions during this period.
required_documents: Valid passport (original + copies)
Completed national visa application form(s)
Biometric photos
Signed employment contract or binding job offer (minimum 6 months duration, matching qualifications, meeting salary thresholds)
Proof of a recognized university degree (or, for IT specialists, at least 3 years of relevant professional experience in the last 7 years)
Detailed CV and, if applicable, employer reference letters
Proof of health insurance cover (travel insurance for visa stage, German statutory or private cover after arrival)
Proof that academic qualification is recognized in Germany (e.g., Anabin database printout or ZAB Statement of Comparability)
Police Clearance Certificate (PCC) (case-by-case basis)
Proof of accommodation (if applying in Germany)

visas.name: Self-employment visa for (Germany)
visas.description: The Germany Self-employment visa (encompassing both 'Freiberufler' for liberal professions and 'Selbständiger/Gewerbetreibender' for commercial self-employment) allows foreign nationals to reside in Germany and work independently. Applicants must demonstrate a viable business idea that serves an economic interest or regional demand in Germany, is expected to have a positive impact on the German economy (e.g., creating jobs, contributing to innovation), and has secured financing.
benefits: Work independently and establish a business in Germany.
Long-term stay, with an initial validity of up to three years.
Provides a clear pathway to permanent residency in Germany.
No employer sponsorship or job offer is required.
Freelancers (Freiberufler) may be exempt from trade tax and business registration.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Holders of a self-employment residence permit can apply for a settlement permit (permanent residency). For entrepreneurs (commercial self-employment), this can be after three years if the business is successful and livelihood is secured. For freelancers (under Section 21 (5) of the Residence Act), a settlement permit can be issued after five years.
required_documents: Completed national visa application form (often online via VIDEX).
Valid passport and two recent biometric passport photos.
Detailed Curriculum Vitae (CV).
Motivation letter or cover letter describing the intended stay and target clients.

Comprehensive business plan (for commercial self-employment) or earnings preview/freelance plan (for liberal professions). This includes a company profile, business concept, capital requirement plan, financing plan, marketing strategy, and revenue forecast.
Proof of sufficient financial means to finance the business and cover living expenses (e.g., bank statements, blocked account, loan commitment, proof of equity capital).
Proof of accommodation in Germany (e.g., rental contract, address registration).
Proof of health insurance (initial travel health insurance, then German statutory or private health insurance).
Proof of professional qualification, such as diplomas, vocational training, professional licenses, or a portfolio of previous work.
Letters of intent or confirmed client contracts (ideally from two or more German clients for freelancers).
Proof of adequate retirement pension provisions if the applicant is over 45 years of age.
Proof of economic interest or regional demand for the business/service and its positive impact on the German economy.
Trade license (Gewerbeschein) if establishing a commercial business (Gewerbetreibender).

visas.name: The EU Blue (Germany)
visas.description: The EU Blue Card for Germany is a combined work-and-residence permit designed for highly qualified non-EU/EEA nationals. It facilitates immigration for individuals with a recognized university degree or, for IT specialists, substantial professional experience, who have a binding job offer in Germany that meets a specific minimum salary threshold.
benefits: Faster path to permanent residency in Germany (21 or 33 months).
Simplified family reunification, allowing spouses to work immediately without German language requirements.
Enhanced mobility within the EU after 12-18 months of residence in a Member State.
Equal treatment with German nationals regarding working conditions, education, and social benefits (e.g., healthcare, unemployment insurance).
Legal entitlement to the permit if all requirements are met, providing planning security.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Holders of an EU Blue Card can apply for a German permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) after 33 months of highly qualified employment and pension contributions with basic German language skills (A1 level). This period is reduced to 21 months if the applicant demonstrates sufficient German language skills (B1 level).
required_documents: Valid passport
Completed national visa application form(s)
Recent biometric passport photos
Signed employment contract or binding job offer (minimum 6 months duration)
Proof of a recognized university degree or evidence of qualifying professional experience (for IT specialists)
Proof of recognition of foreign degree (e.g., Anabin database printout or ZAB Statement of Comparability)
Curriculum Vitae (CV)
Proof of health insurance (travel insurance for visa stage, German statutory/private cover after arrival)
Declaration of employment signed by your employer (Erklärung zum Beschäftigungsverhältnis)
If applicable, professional license for regulated professions

visas.name: Germany Student Visa (Studentenvisum)
visas.description: The Germany Student Visa (Studentenvisum) is a national (D-visa) required for non-EU/EEA citizens planning to pursue long-term academic studies at recognized higher education institutions in Germany. It allows entry for study purposes, initially for 3-6 months, which must then be converted into a residence permit for the duration of studies upon arrival in Germany.
benefits: Access to world-class education with low or no tuition fees.
Opportunity to work part-time during studies.
Post-study 18-month job-seeking visa.
Clear pathway to permanent residency and potential citizenship.
High visa success rate for well-prepared applicants.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After completing a degree from a recognized German university, students can apply for an 18-month Job-Seeking Visa. Upon securing a job related to their qualification, they can switch to a work residence permit or an EU Blue Card. Permanent Residency (Settlement Permit) can be applied for after 2 years of full-time skilled employment (with B1 German language skills and an EU Blue Card) or 33 months (without Blue Card or B1 German).
required_documents: Completed and signed national visa application form (with two copies).
Valid passport (issued within the last 10 years, valid for at least 6 months beyond intended stay, with at least two blank pages) and two copies of the data page.
Recent biometric passport photographs (typically 3, 35x45mm, white background, not older than 3 months).
Letter of acceptance or conditional acceptance from a German university/higher education institution.

Proof of financial resources, typically a blocked account (Sperrkonto) showing a minimum of €11,904 for one year (€992 per month) for 2025/2026. Alternatives include a scholarship award letter or a formal obligation letter (Verpflichtungserklärung) by a sponsor in Germany.
Proof of health insurance coverage (travel health insurance for initial entry, then statutory student health insurance).
Academic transcripts and qualifications (school-leaving certificates, university degrees, grades, often with authenticated copies).
Curriculum Vitae (CV).
Motivation letter or statement of purpose outlining study plans and goals.
Proof of German or English language proficiency (minimum B2 level CEFR, depending on the language of instruction).
Proof of payment for the visa application fee.
APS (Akademische Prüfstelle) certificate for students from certain countries (e.g., India, China, Vietnam).

visas.name: Germany Family Reunion Visa
visas.description: The Germany Family Reunion Visa allows non-EU/EEA citizens to join close family members (spouse, registered partner, children under 18, and in some cases parents) who are German citizens or legal residents in Germany. The visa is initially an entry visa (National D visa) which then needs to be converted into a residence permit upon arrival in Germany for long-term stay. [2, 4, 19, 22, 24]
benefits: Legal pathway to live with family in Germany. [2]
Access to healthcare system. [2]
Education opportunities for children. [2]
Right to work in Germany (after obtaining residence permit). [4, 9, 25]
Counts towards long-term settlement, permanent residency, and citizenship. [2, 22]
visas.path_to_residency_description: After 3 years of legal residence in Germany on a family reunion residence permit, family members may apply for a settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis), which grants permanent residence, provided other conditions are met (e.g., marriage or family relationship still exists, sufficient income and housing). [2, 22]
required_documents: Valid passport (issued within last 10 years, at least 6 months validity, 2 blank pages). [2, 7, 16]
Two biometric passport photos (no older than 3 months). [3, 7]
Completed visa application form. [3, 7]
Proof of relationship (e.g., legalized/apostilled marriage certificate for spouses, birth certificate for children, translated into German). [2, 3, 4, 7]
Sponsor's valid residence permit or German citizenship proof. [2, 3, 7]
Sponsor's employment contract and recent payslips (3-6 months) showing sufficient income. [3, 4, 7]
Sponsor's rental agreement showing adequate living space for the family. [3, 4, 7]
Proof of health insurance coverage (for the applicant and sponsor). [2, 3, 7, 11]
Proof of basic German language skills (A1 level) for spouses, unless exempt. [2, 3, 4, 6, 7]
Clean criminal record (if applicable). [7, 18]
Travel health insurance for the first 90 days of stay with minimum coverage of €30,000. [5, 6, 11]
Visa fee payment receipt. [3, 4]

visas.name: Germany Opportunity Card (Chancenkarte)
visas.description: The Germany Opportunity Card (Chancenkarte) is a residence permit under Section 20a of the German Residence Act, designed to allow skilled non-EU nationals to enter Germany to search for qualified employment or qualification measures without a prior job offer. Applicants can qualify either as a recognized skilled worker or by achieving a minimum of six points in a points-based system.
benefits: Access to the German job market for up to one year without a pre-arranged job offer.
Ability to work part-time (up to 20 hours per week) and undertake trial jobs for up to two weeks per employer while job searching.
Provides a pathway to transition to a long-term residence permit (e.g., work permit or EU Blue Card) and eventually permanent residency.
Simplified entry procedures for qualified professionals compared to previous immigration routes.
Entitles holders to travel within the Schengen area once issued.
visas.path_to_residency_description: The Opportunity Card itself is not a permanent visa but acts as a stepping stone. Once qualified employment is secured, holders can transition to a German Work Permit or an EU Blue Card. Eligibility for permanent residency (Niederlassungserlaubnis) typically requires 21-33 months of employment for EU Blue Card holders (with B1 German proficiency) or 4-5 years for standard work permit holders. Time spent on the Opportunity Card counts towards the required residence duration for permanent residency.
required_documents: Valid Passport
Completed and signed visa application form (e.g., Videx form)
Recent biometric passport photos
Curriculum Vitae (CV)
Cover letter explaining job search plans
Proof of qualifications (university degree or at least two years of vocational training, recognized in country of origin or partially recognized in Germany)
Proof of financial means (minimum €1,091 per month, typically €13,092 per year, e.g., blocked account, part-time job contract, or sponsorship)
Proof of German language skills (minimum A1) or English language skills (minimum B2)
Proof of adequate health insurance coverage
Proof of work experience (if applicable, for points system)
Proof of previous legal stay in Germany (if applicable, for points system)
Proof of residence (e.g., Melde-Bestätigung) or living space (if applying from within Germany)

visas.name: Germany Job Seeker Visa
visas.description: The Germany Job Seeker Visa (Section 20 German Residence Act) allows qualified professionals from non-EU countries to enter Germany for up to six months to search for employment that matches their qualifications. If successful in securing a job, the visa holder can then apply for a work permit or an EU Blue Card without having to leave Germany. The visa is typically issued for a maximum of 6 months and is not extendable in its original form.
benefits: Opportunity to search for qualified employment in Germany for up to 6 months.
Ability to convert to a work permit or EU Blue Card upon securing a job offer in Germany without leaving the country.
Allows travel within the Schengen area for up to 90 days within 180 days for tourism purposes.
Permits taking up part-time or casual work during the job search period (some sources say any type of employment, others imply it is restricted to qualified roles).
Access to a strong economy and high quality of life if employment is secured.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Upon securing qualified employment in Germany, the Job Seeker Visa can be converted into a Residence Permit for Employment or an EU Blue Card. These subsequent residence permits can then lead to permanent residency. For example, an EU Blue Card holder can obtain permanent residency after 33 months of employment (or 21 months with B1 German proficiency).
required_documents: Completed visa application form.
Valid passport (issued within the past 10 years, valid for entire intended stay, with at least two blank pages).
Two recent biometric passport-sized photographs.
Professional CV (Curriculum Vitae) detailing academic background, work experience, and relevant skills.
Motivation letter explaining the planned course of action to secure a job (sector, region, accommodation) and any evidence of preparations.
Proof of academic qualification (recognized university degree or vocational training equivalent to a German degree). If applicable, proof of recognition from ANABIN.
Proof of sufficient financial means to cover living costs for the duration of stay (e.g., blocked account showing approximately €7,200 for six months or a Declaration of Commitment).
Proof of valid health insurance covering the entire stay, with a minimum coverage of €30,000 for medical expenses.
Proof of accommodation in Germany.
Declaration of accuracy of information.
Proof of current residence permit (if applying from within a country that allows it, e.g., US, UK, Canada, Australia, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, and Korea).
Proof of address (e.g., valid driver's license, utility bill, lease, or registration of address 'Meldebescheinigung' if already in Germany).

visas.name: Germany Self-Employment Visa
visas.description: The Germany Self-Employment Visa (also known as the Freelance Visa, under Section 21 of the Residence Act - AufenthG) allows non-EU citizens to live and work independently in Germany. It caters to two main categories: 'Freiberufler' (liberal professions like artists, journalists, engineers, IT consultants, doctors, lawyers) and 'Gewerbetreibender' (commercial business owners). Applicants must demonstrate a viable business idea, secured financing, and the ability to cover living costs. For commercial businesses, there must be an economic interest or regional demand and a positive impact on the German economy. For liberal professions, the focus is on professional qualifications and the viability of the freelance activity.
benefits: Live and work independently in Germany for up to three years, with possibility of extension.
Opportunity to travel freely within the Schengen Area.
Option to work for both German and international clients/companies.
Path to permanent residency after 3-5 years and eventual German citizenship.
Flexible work modes and potential for tax deductions for business expenses.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After 3-5 years of successful self-employment and continuous residence, applicants can apply for a settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis), provided they meet requirements such as sufficient income, German language proficiency (typically B1), adequate pension provisions, and basic civic knowledge. German citizenship may be applied for after 5 years of residence with exceptional integration, or 8 years normally.
required_documents: Completed application form (VIDEX).
Valid passport and two biometric passport photos.
Detailed business plan/concept (including capital requirement plan, financing plan, revenue forecast).
Proof of sufficient funds to finance the business and cover living expenses (e.g., bank statements, blocked account, loan commitments).
Proof of health insurance valid in Germany.
Curriculum Vitae (CV) detailing educational and professional experience.
Proof of professional qualifications (degrees, certifications, licenses if required for the profession).
Proof of accommodation in Germany (e.g., rental agreement).
Letters of intent or confirmed client contracts (especially for 'Freiberufler').
Proof of adequate pension provisions if over 45 years of age.

visas.name: EU Blue Card
visas.description: The EU Blue Card is a combined work and residence permit for highly qualified non-EU/EEA nationals seeking employment in Germany. It facilitates the immigration of skilled workers with academic qualifications or specific professional experience into the German labor market.
visas.target_applicant: Highly skilled professionals from non-EU/EEA countries with a recognized university degree or comparable qualification, who have a binding job offer in Germany meeting specific salary thresholds.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Holders can apply for a settlement permit (permanent residency) after 33 months of highly qualified employment and pension contributions with A1 German language skills. This period reduces to 21 months with B1 German language skills.
visas.renewal_conditions: Must continue to meet conditions, including salary thresholds and skilled employment; usually issued for the duration of the employment contract plus three months.
benefits: Fast-track path to permanent residency (21 months with B1 German, 33 months with A1 German).
Simplified family reunification, allowing spouses and minor children to join and spouses to work immediately without German language requirements.
Mobility rights within the EU after 12 months of residence on a Blue Card in one Member State.
Ability to switch employers or positions without always needing to amend the permit after initial 12 months.
Visa-free travel within the Schengen Area for up to 90 days within a 180-day period.
required_documents: Valid passport
Completed national visa application form(s) and biometric photos
Signed employment contract or binding job offer (minimum 6 months duration) matching qualifications
Proof of a recognized university degree or evidence of qualifying professional experience (e.g., Anabin database printout, ZAB Statement of Comparability)
Curriculum vitae (CV) and, where relevant, employer reference letters
Proof of health insurance cover (travel insurance for visa stage, German statutory or private cover after arrival)
Proof of accommodation plans in Germany (if requested)
Declaration of employment signed by employer ('Erklärung zum Beschäftigungsverhältnis')
Official permission to practice profession (if applicable, for regulated professions)
application_process_steps: Secure a qualified job offer in Germany.
Ensure your academic qualification is recognized in Germany (e.g., via Anabin database or ZAB Statement of Comparability).
Apply for a national visa (Type D) at the German embassy or consulate in your home country, submitting all required documents and biometrics.
Enter Germany with the national visa.
Register your address at the local Residents' Registration Office (Anmeldung).
Apply for the physical EU Blue Card residence permit at the local Foreigners' Authority (Ausländerbehörde).

visas.name: Work Visa for Qualified Professionals (Skilled Worker Visa)
visas.description: The Work Visa for Qualified Professionals (Skilled Worker Visa) in Germany is designed for non-EU citizens with recognized vocational training or a university degree, or significant professional experience, who have a concrete job offer from a German employer. It allows individuals to live and work in Germany in a qualified position, contributing to sectors facing skilled labor shortages.
visas.target_applicant: The ideal applicant is a non-EU citizen with either a recognized university degree, qualified vocational training, or at least two years of relevant professional experience, who has secured a job offer in Germany in a field matching their qualifications.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Skilled workers with an academic degree can obtain a settlement permit (permanent residence) after three years of employment in Germany. Those with vocational training or foreign qualifications (under the Skilled Immigration Act) may also be eligible for permanent residency after several years of employment, with some sources indicating 3-4 years.
visas.renewal_conditions: Typically requires maintaining employment in Germany and continuing to meet the eligibility criteria of the visa.
benefits: Access to Europe's largest economy and a strong job market.
Path to permanent residency and eventually citizenship.
Ability to bring immediate family members (spouse, minor children, and in some cases parents) to Germany.
Good quality of life, strong healthcare system, and work-life balance.
Allows work in Germany in a qualified position.
required_documents: Valid passport (issued within the last 10 years, with at least 2 blank pages, valid for at least 3 months beyond intended stay).
Completed long-stay visa application form.
Two recent biometric passport-sized photos.
Signed employment contract or binding job offer letter from a German employer (stating role, salary, working hours, and start date).
Degree certificates or vocational qualification certificates (originals and certified copies).
Proof that qualifications are recognized in Germany (e.g., ANABIN verification, Statement of Comparability, ZAB evaluation, or recognition from home country for §19c).
Updated CV.
Motivation letter explaining career goals.
Proof of accommodation in Germany.
Proof of financial means (if required, for initial stay before first salary).
Valid health insurance documents (covering the period from entry until employment starts, then statutory or comprehensive private health insurance).
Clean criminal record certificate.
Visa fee payment confirmation.
Employer's 'Declaration of Employment' (usually required).
application_process_steps: Secure a job offer from a German employer that matches your qualification.
Check for recognition of your foreign qualification via the ANABIN database, ZAB, or official recognition portals.
Gather all required documents, ensuring they are complete and translated if necessary.
Apply online via the Consular Services Portal of the German Federal Foreign Office, completing the application form and uploading supporting documents for preliminary review.

Book and attend an in-person appointment at the German embassy or consulate in your home country (or local foreigners' authority if already in Germany) to submit original documents, provide biometrics, and pay the visa fee.
Receive the visa, enter Germany, and register your address, then apply for the residence permit at the local immigration office (Ausländerbehörde) after arrival.

visas.name: Visa for Professionally Experienced Workers
visas.description: This visa is designed for non-EU citizens who possess a foreign academic degree or vocational training qualification and at least two years of relevant professional experience. It allows them to obtain a residence permit to work in Germany in a non-regulated profession, addressing the country's labor shortages. For applicants over 45 years old, a higher annual gross salary threshold or proof of adequate pension provision is required.
visas.target_applicant: The ideal applicant is a skilled professional from a non-EU country with a recognized academic or vocational qualification and substantial work experience, who has secured a job offer in a non-regulated profession in Germany.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Foreign professionals who hold this residence permit for at least three years may be eligible for a settlement permit (permanent residency). This period can be shortened to 21 months if a higher level of German language skills (B1) and contributions to the pension fund are proven.
visas.renewal_conditions: The residence permit can be extended based on continued employment status. If over 45, the gross annual salary must meet a higher threshold of at least €55,770 (as of 2026) or adequate pension provision must be proven.
benefits: Facilitates immigration for skilled workers to Germany.
Provides a clear pathway to permanent residency in Germany.
Does not always require formal recognition of foreign qualifications in Germany for non-regulated professions, only recognition by the issuing country.
No mandatory German language proficiency for many roles, although beneficial.
required_documents: Valid passport (issued within the last 10 years, with at least 2 blank pages and valid for at least one year from visa issue date).
Completed long-stay visa application form (e.g., VIDEX).
Biometric passport-sized photos (3.5 x 4.5 cm with a light background).
Signed employment contract or concrete job offer letter from a German employer in a non-regulated profession.
Academic degree certificates or vocational training diplomas (qualification recognized by the country of issuance, vocational training must be at least two years).
Proof of qualification recognition (e.g., ZAB evaluation, ANABIN printout, or Statement of Comparability).
Curriculum Vitae (CV) and professional experience references demonstrating at least two years of qualified professional experience within the last five years.
Proof of accommodation in Germany.
Proof of financial means (if required for initial stay, though a job offer usually covers this).
Valid health insurance documents.
Declaration of Employment ('Erklärung zum Beschäftigungsverhältnis') form completed by the employer.
Motivation letter explaining career goals.
application_process_steps: Confirm recognition or comparability of your qualification (e.g., via ZAB or ANABIN).
Secure a concrete job offer in a qualified, non-regulated profession from a German employer, ensuring the salary meets the minimum requirements.
Gather and prepare all required documents, including the completed Declaration of Employment from your employer.
Apply for an entry visa at the German mission (embassy or consulate) in your home country, or at your local foreigners' authority if you are already legally in Germany.
Attend the visa appointment, submit biometrics, and pay the application fee. During this process, the Federal Employment Agency (BA) will typically approve your employment.
Upon approval, receive the visa, enter Germany, register your address, and then apply for the residence permit at your local immigration office (Ausländerbehörde).

visas.name: Job Seeker Visa (Chancenkarte / Opportunity Card)
visas.description: The 'Chancenkarte', or Opportunity Card, is a residence permit for non-EU nationals allowing them to live in Germany for up to one year to find qualified employment. It facilitates entry into the German job market by permitting part-time work and trial jobs during the job search period.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are skilled professionals from non-EU/EEA countries with either a recognized qualification or sufficient points based on criteria like education, language skills, and work experience, who wish to seek employment in Germany without a prior job offer.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Upon securing qualified employment that meets residence permit requirements, Opportunity Card holders can transition to a standard residence permit for employment or an EU Blue Card, which eventually leads to permanent residence and citizenship.
visas.renewal_conditions: Can be extended by up to two additional years if a qualified job offer is secured but transition to a standard residence permit is not yet possible; application must be made at the local Foreigners' Registration Office.
benefits: Allows entry to Germany to search for a job without a pre-existing employment contract
Permits part-time work for up to 20 hours per week while job seeking
Allows trial jobs for up to two weeks with prospective employers
Provides a pathway to long-term residence and eventually permanent residency in Germany
Simplifies entry conditions for prospective workers from non-EU countries
required_documents: Valid Passport (valid for at least three months beyond intended stay, with blank pages)
Completed and Signed Visa Application Form
Recent Biometric Passport Photo
Proof of Residence
Cover Letter Explaining Job Search Plans
Curriculum Vitae (CV)
Proof of Qualifications (university degree or at least two years of vocational training)
Proof of Recognition (if applicable, e.g., Statement of Comparability from ZAB)
Proof of Work Experience (if applicable)
Proof of Financial Means (e.g., blocked account, declaration of commitment, or part-time employment contract for €1,091/month)
Proof of Language Skills (A1 German or B2 English, official certificates required)
Proof of Health Insurance (valid German statutory or comparable private health insurance)
Partner and family documents (if applicable)
application_process_steps: Check eligibility criteria and accumulate at least six points (unless qualifying as a recognized skilled worker)
Gather all required documents, including passport, qualifications, financial proof, and language certificates
Complete and sign the visa application form, potentially online via the Federal Foreign Office website
Submit the application at the competent German embassy or consulate in your country of origin, or at the local Foreigners' Registration Office if already in Germany
Wait for approval, with processing times varying depending on the application location
Upon arrival in Germany, register your residence at the local registration office (Bürgeramt) within 14 days and begin your job search

visas.name: General Employment Visa
visas.description: The General Employment Visa in Germany allows non-EU citizens with a job offer from a German employer to live and work in Germany. It requires the applicant to possess recognized qualifications and leads to a residence permit, with a clear path to permanent residency.
visas.target_applicant: Non-EU citizens who have secured a binding employment contract or job offer from a German employer and possess professional qualifications recognized in Germany.
visas.path_to_residency_description: General employment visa holders can apply for permanent residency (Settlement Permit) after 5 years of legal residence in Germany with a valid temporary residence permit. EU Blue Card holders (a specific type of employment visa) can apply after 33 months, or 21 months if they demonstrate B1 German language proficiency. Graduates from German universities can apply after two years of employment in a job related to their degree.
visas.renewal_conditions: Maintaining employment, meeting income thresholds, and making social security/pension contributions.
benefits: Ability to live and work legally in Germany
Opportunity to bring dependants (spouse and children)
Path to permanent residency in Germany
Multiple entries to Germany
required_documents: Valid passport (issued within the last 10 years, with at least two blank pages, and valid for at least another year from application date)
Two completed national visa application forms
Two biometric passport-sized photographs (not older than 6 months)
Signed employment contract or job offer letter from a German employer
Proof that qualifications are recognized in Germany (e.g., ANABIN verification or statement of comparability)
Curriculum Vitae (CV)
Motivation letter (explaining career goals and reasons for working in Germany)
Proof of accommodation in Germany
Proof of financial means (typically covered by the employment contract/salary)
Proof of compulsory health insurance from a German employer (and possibly travel health insurance for the initial period before employment starts)
Clean criminal record certificate
Visa application fee payment confirmation
application_process_steps: Secure a binding employment contract or job offer from a German employer.
Check for recognition of your foreign professional qualifications in Germany (e.g., via ANABIN database).
Gather all required documents for the visa application, ensuring two identical sets.
Complete the national visa application form (available online via the Consular Services Portal).
Book an appointment at the German Embassy or Consulate in your home country and attend in person to submit documents and provide biometric data.
Pay the visa application fee at the time of your appointment.

visas.name: Visa for Self-Employment (Entrepreneur Visa)
visas.description: This visa program is for foreign nationals who intend to establish and operate a business in Germany as a self-employed individual, either as an entrepreneur (setting up a company) or as a freelancer (working independently in a liberal profession). It allows them to reside and work independently in Germany.
visas.target_applicant: Non-EU/EEA/Swiss citizens who possess a viable business idea demonstrating economic interest or regional demand in Germany, can prove sufficient financial means to fund their business and livelihood, and potentially have relevant professional qualifications or experience.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After three years of successfully operating the business, holders of the self-employment visa may apply for a settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis), which grants permanent residency in Germany. To qualify, applicants must demonstrate sustainable business operations, sufficient income to support their livelihood without public assistance, and German language skills (typically A2 level). After 6-8 years of legal residency, or 5 years with strong integration efforts (e.g., advanced German language proficiency, civic engagement), one can apply for full German citizenship.
visas.renewal_conditions: The residence permit can be extended if the business idea is successful and the applicant is able to cover the costs of living for themselves and their family. Renewal requires demonstrating ongoing economic activity and viability of the business. If over 45, continued proof of adequate old-age pension provision is required, which may include maintaining a specific monthly pension (e.g., €1,332.36 or €1,340.47) or assets (e.g., €194,631 or €195,104.00) by age 67.
visas.tax_implications: Standard German resident tax rules apply to individuals and their businesses. No specific special tax treatments or exemptions are mentioned for this visa category.
benefits: Opportunity to establish and run a business in Germany, Europe's largest economy.
Long-term residency in Germany, initially for up to three years.
Clear pathway to permanent residency (settlement permit) after 3 years of successful business activity.
Potential for German citizenship after 5-8 years of legal residency.
Freedom to work independently without an employer in Germany.
required_documents: Completed application form (VIDEX online form recommended)
Valid passport (original and copies, valid for at least six months with at least two blank pages)
Two recent biometric passport photos (not older than 3-6 months)
Curriculum Vitae (CV) detailing educational and professional experience
Business plan (comprehensive, including company profile, business concept, capital requirement, financing plan, marketing strategy, revenue forecast, impact on German economy/labour market)
Financing plan or proof of secured financing (own capital or loan commitment)
Proof of financial means to cover living expenses in Germany (e.g., blocked account, bank statements, sponsorship letter)
Proof of accommodation in Germany
Proof of health insurance valid in Germany
Proof of professional qualifications (e.g., diplomas, vocational training, professional licenses)
For freelancers: At least two letters of intent for collaboration from prospective German clients
If over 45 years of age: Proof of adequate old-age pension provision (e.g., private pension plan, life insurance, own funds, business assets)
application_process_steps: Check eligibility and gather all required documents, including a comprehensive business plan and proof of financial means.
Complete the online national visa application form (VIDEX) and print it out.
Schedule an appointment at the competent German embassy or consulate in your country of residence.
Submit your application in person with all original documents and required copies, and pay the visa fee.
Receive the entry visa; upon arrival in Germany, register your address with local authorities within two weeks.
Apply for the residence permit for self-employment at the local Foreigners' Office (Ausländerbehörde) before your entry visa expires.

visas.name: Freelance Visa (Freiberufler Visa)
visas.description: The Freelance Visa (Freiberufler Visa) program in Germany allows non-EU/EEA citizens to reside and work independently as self-employed professionals in 'liberal professions' such as IT, consulting, translation, design, and artistic fields. This visa permits individuals to offer their services to clients and operate their own businesses within Germany.
visas.target_applicant: The ideal applicant is a non-EU/EEA citizen with recognized professional qualifications or expertise, a viable freelance plan, and demonstrable financial resources to sustain themselves through freelance work in Germany.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After 5 years of continuous legal residence on a freelance visa, applicants may apply for a 'Niederlassungserlaubnis' (permanent settlement permit). Requirements include B1 level German language proficiency, demonstrated financial stability, at least 60 months of pension contributions, and a clean criminal record. German citizenship is generally possible after 8 years of residence, or 5 years with exceptional integration (e.g., C1 German language skills), provided other naturalization criteria are met.
visas.renewal_conditions: To renew the residence permit, applicants must demonstrate continued successful freelance activity, maintain financial stability to cover living expenses, and continue to meet general immigration requirements.
visas.tax_implications: Freelancers ('Freiberufler') are subject to progressive income tax rates (from 0% up to 45% for higher earners, with a basic tax-free allowance of €12,348 for 2026). Most freelancers are also liable for Value Added Tax (VAT - Umsatzsteuer) at a standard rate of 19% (or 7% for certain professions), unless they qualify for the 'Kleinunternehmerregelung' (small business regulation) for lower annual turnovers. 'Freiberufler' are generally exempt from trade tax ('Gewerbesteuer') and do not need to register with the trade office. Income tax is typically paid in quarterly advance payments based on estimated annual income.
benefits: Legal right to live and work as a freelancer in Germany.
Opportunity to collaborate with diverse clients and establish a business in a major European economy.
Provides a clear path to permanent residency after 5 years and German citizenship after 5-8 years of continuous residence.
Allows for family reunification, enabling spouses and children to join the visa holder.
Grants freedom of travel within the Schengen Area without requiring additional visas.
required_documents: Completed visa application form and biometric passport pictures.
Valid passport with at least three empty pages and sufficient validity beyond the intended stay.
Up-to-date Curriculum Vitae (CV).
Detailed freelance plan or business plan, including projected income and expenditure, often for the first three years.
Proof of professional qualifications (e.g., degrees, certifications, vocational training, professional authorizations). Foreign qualifications may require German translation and recognition.
At least two letters of intent or commitment from potential clients, demonstrating a demand for your services and proving future income.
Proof of sufficient financial means to cover living costs (e.g., bank statements, revenue forecast, proof of savings).
Proof of local accommodation in Germany (e.g., rental contract, registration of address 'Anmeldung').
Proof of comprehensive health, care, and (if over 45) pension insurance valid in Germany. Travel insurance is typically only accepted for initial entry.
If applicable, proof of German language knowledge (though not always mandatory for the visa, it can be beneficial).
A cover letter outlining your professional activities, reasons for choosing Germany, and target clientele.
application_process_steps: Determine if your intended freelance profession qualifies as a 'Freiberufler' under German law and gather all necessary documentation.
Prepare a comprehensive freelance/business plan and obtain letters of intent from at least two potential clients.
Apply for the national visa (Type D) at the German embassy or consulate in your country of residence (online submission may be available in some locations like Berlin from March 2026).
Pay the application fee for the national visa.
Upon approval and issuance of the D-visa, travel to Germany.
Within two weeks of arrival, register your residential address (Anmeldung) and open a German bank account.
Register your self-employment with the local tax office (Finanzamt) to obtain a tax number (Steuernummer).
Before your initial D-visa expires, apply for the longer-term residence permit for freelancers at the local immigration office (Ausländerbehörde).

visas.name: Business Investor Visa
visas.description: The 'Business Investor Visa' in Germany is formally known as a Residence Permit for Self-Employment (Aufenthaltserlaubnis zur selbständigen Tätigkeit) under Section 21 of the German Residence Act. It allows non-EU nationals to establish, manage, or invest in a business in Germany. The visa is granted based on the economic viability and regional benefit of the proposed business activity, rather than on academic qualifications or a salary threshold.
visas.target_applicant: The ideal applicant is a non-EU national who wishes to found a new business, manage an existing German company as a director or shareholder, or invest significantly in a German enterprise, demonstrating a viable business idea with economic interest or regional demand.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Entrepreneurs can transition to a permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) after 3 years of continuous residence if the business demonstrates stability, consistent operations, tax compliance, and provides sufficient income and social security coverage, along with at least A2-level German language proficiency. Freelancers typically qualify after 5 years.
visas.renewal_conditions: The business idea must remain successful, the applicant must be able to make a living for themselves and their family, and maintain health insurance and social security coverage.
benefits: Opportunity to establish and manage a business in Europe's largest economy.
Path to permanent residency after 3 years of successful business operation.
Ability to bring dependants (spouse and children) who can work or study.
Access to a stable pro-business environment and advanced industrial infrastructure.
Visa-free entry to all Schengen countries once residency is granted.
required_documents: Completed application form (national visa D)
Valid passport (issued within the last 10 years, valid for at least 6 months, with at least one blank double page)
Biometric passport photographs
Comprehensive business plan (including company profile, business concept, financing plan with 3-year capital, liquidity, and revenue forecast)
Proof of secured financing (own capital or credible loan commitment)
Proof of health insurance (German statutory or equivalent private policy)
Proof of accommodation (e.g., rental contract, address registration)
Curriculum Vitae (CV) with detailed professional career, qualification certificates, and references
Proof of adequate old-age pension provision (if over 45 years old)
Documents demonstrating no criminal record
Professional licenses or qualifications relevant to the proposed business activity (if applicable)
application_process_steps: Check qualification criteria, ensuring the business idea meets economic interest or regional demand and has a positive impact on the German economy.
Gather all required documents, including a detailed business plan, financing proof, passport, photos, and health insurance.
Submit the national visa (Type D) application for self-employment at the German embassy or consulate in the country of origin or permanent residence.
Enter Germany with the national visa and register the address with the local authority within 14 days of arrival.
Apply for the residence permit for self-employment at the local Foreigners Authority (Ausländerbehörde) before the entry visa expires.
Attend a personal appointment at the Foreigners Authority to submit documents and potentially receive the residence permit.

visas.name: German Student Visa
visas.description: The German Student Visa (National Visa D) is for international students from non-EU/EEA/Swiss countries who plan to pursue long-term academic studies at a recognized higher education institution in Germany. It allows the holder to enter Germany and subsequently apply for a residence permit for the duration of their studies.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are individuals who have received an acceptance letter from a German university or are applying for a university place and need to prepare for their studies in Germany.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Upon successful completion of studies, graduates can apply for an 18-month Job Seeker Visa. After securing qualified employment, they can transition to a Work Visa or EU Blue Card. Permanent residency (Niederlassungserlaubnis) can be obtained after 21-33 months of qualified employment with an EU Blue Card (with B1 German proficiency) or after 5 years with a standard work permit. German citizenship is possible after 6-8 years of residence.
visas.renewal_conditions: Must maintain student status, demonstrate continued sufficient financial resources, and hold valid health insurance. The residence permit is typically renewed for two-year periods for the duration of studies.
benefits: Opportunity to pursue higher education at German universities.
Ability to work part-time during studies to support living costs.
Clear pathway to permanent residency and ultimately citizenship after graduation and employment in Germany.
Initial visa allows entry, which is then converted into a renewable residence permit for the duration of studies.
required_documents: Completed visa application form (often via VIDEX portal)
Valid passport (original and copies, valid for at least three months beyond intended stay, with at least two blank pages)
Two current biometric passport photos
Acceptance letter (Zulassungsbescheinigung) from a German university or a conditional admission letter/proof of application for a study place
Proof of financial resources (e.g., blocked account showing €11,904 per year or €992 per month for 2025/2026, or a declaration of commitment from a sponsor, or scholarship confirmation)
Proof of health insurance (travel health insurance for initial entry, then statutory or approved private student health insurance)
Academic certificates and qualifications (school-leaving certificate, university degrees, transcripts, etc.)
Proof of German or English language proficiency (depending on the language of instruction)
Curriculum Vitae (CV)
Motivation letter/Statement of purpose
APS (Academic Evaluation Centre) certificate for applicants from certain countries (e.g., China, Vietnam, India)
application_process_steps: Complete the online visa application form via the Consular Services Portal (VIDEX) and print it out.

Gather all required documents, including passport, biometric photos, admission letter, proof of finances, health insurance, and academic records. Ensure documents not in German or English are translated and certified.
Book an appointment at the competent German embassy or consulate in your home country.
Attend the visa interview, submit all original documents along with copies, provide biometric data, and pay the visa application fee.
Wait for the visa decision (processing typically takes 6 to 8 weeks, but can extend to 3 months or more depending on location and season).

Upon arrival in Germany, register your address with the Resident Registration Office (Einwohnermeldeamt) and apply for a residence permit at the local Foreigners' Office (Ausländerbehörde) to cover the full duration of your studies.

visas.name: Student Applicant Visa
visas.description: The Student Applicant Visa (Visum zur Studienbewerbung) allows prospective international students to enter Germany to prepare for and apply to universities. It is intended for individuals who have not yet received an official university admission letter but intend to pursue higher education in Germany. This visa enables applicants to fulfill admission requirements, attend entrance exams, or enroll in preparatory courses like Studienkolleg or intensive language courses within Germany.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are non-EU/EEA citizens who have completed secondary education and meet German university entry academic requirements, actively seeking admission to a German university or preparatory program but lacking a final acceptance letter.
visas.path_to_residency_description: Upon gaining admission to a German university, the student applicant visa can be converted into a student residence permit from within Germany. After completing studies and finding qualified employment, individuals can apply for an EU Blue Card or a general employment visa, which can lead to permanent residency after 5 years (half the time spent as a student in Germany will be recognized).
visas.renewal_conditions: The visa can be extended by up to 6 additional months at the local Foreigners' Office (Ausländerbehörde) for a total maximum of 9 months, requiring continued proof of active university applications and sufficient financial resources.
benefits: Allows entry into Germany without a prior university acceptance letter.
Provides time to apply to universities, attend entrance exams, interviews, or preparatory courses (e.g., Studienkolleg, intensive language courses) in Germany.
Permits conversion to a full student residence permit within Germany once university admission is secured, without needing to leave the country.
Allows part-time work for up to 20 hours per week while holding the visa.
Provides a pathway to permanent residency after successful completion of studies and subsequent employment.
required_documents: Completed national visa application form (2 copies, signed).
Valid passport (issued within the last 10 years, at least 2 blank pages, valid for at least 3 months beyond intended stay).
Two current biometric passport photos.
School-leaving certificate/high school diploma (certified copy + German or English translation).
University degree certificate, if applicable (certified + translated).
Proof of university applications or correspondence with admissions offices (e.g., confirmations, email correspondence, list of universities applied to, registration for entrance exams).
Letter of motivation explaining study plans and goals.
Academic CV.

Proof of financial resources (e.g., blocked account 'Sperrkonto' with €11,904 for 12 months, scholarship award certificate covering at least €992/month, or a formal declaration of commitment from a sponsor living in Germany).
Proof of health insurance (preliminary health insurance covering the first 3 months in Germany, typically travel insurance meeting Schengen requirements).
Proof of accommodation in Germany (e.g., hotel booking, student housing confirmation, rental contract).
Language proficiency certificate, if applicable (e.g., TestDaF, DSH, IELTS, or proof of enrollment in a language course related to planned studies).
APS certificate (mandatory for students from India, China, and Vietnam).
application_process_steps: Prepare all required documents, including proof of academic qualifications, financial resources (e.g., blocked account), health insurance, and evidence of active university applications or preparatory course enrollment. For certain nationalities (India, China, Vietnam), obtain an APS certificate.
Complete and sign the national visa application form (in duplicate).
Schedule an appointment at the German embassy or consulate in your home country.
Attend the visa interview, submitting all original documents and copies. Pay the application fee.
Wait for the visa processing; this can take several weeks to months.

Upon arrival in Germany, register your address with the local residents' registration office (Bürgerbüro) within 14 days and convert preliminary health insurance to statutory or private student health insurance.

visas.name: Language Course Visa (for courses > 3 months)
visas.description: This is a national visa designed for non-EU/EEA nationals who wish to reside in Germany for more than three months to attend an intensive German language course. The visa permits individuals to fully immerse themselves in language learning, with courses requiring at least 18 lessons per week.
visas.target_applicant: Non-EU/EEA nationals who have been admitted to an intensive German language course with a minimum of 18 hours of instruction per week and intend to stay for longer than three months.
visas.path_to_residency_description: While the language course visa itself does not directly lead to permanent residency, it allows for a legal stay in Germany, during which applicants can transition to other long-term visa types (such as a student visa under § 16b, a job-seeker visa, or a Chancenkarte) without needing to leave the country. These subsequent visa types can eventually lead to eligibility for permanent residency or citizenship in Germany.
visas.renewal_conditions: The language course visa itself is generally not renewable beyond its maximum 12-month validity. However, holders may transition to other types of residence permits or visas (e.g., student visa for university studies, job-seeker visa, or Chancenkarte) while remaining in Germany, provided they meet the specific requirements for the new visa category.
benefits: Live and study German intensively in Germany for up to one year.
Opportunity to travel within the Schengen Area.
Permits part-time employment for up to 20 hours per week (excluding self-employment).
Allows for potential transition to other visa types (e.g., student, job-seeker, Chancenkarte) within Germany after the course.
Provides a temporary residence permit in Germany.
required_documents: Duly completed and signed national visa application form (D-visa)
Valid passport (issued within the last 10 years, with at least two empty pages, valid for at least 3 months beyond planned stay) and copies of data page
Two recent biometric passport-sized photos (35x45mm)
Admission or enrollment confirmation from a recognized intensive German language school (detailing course duration, hours, and target proficiency level, minimum 18 lessons/week)

Proof of sufficient financial means (e.g., blocked account with at least €1,091 per month or a formal obligation letter (Verpflichtungserklärung) from a sponsor in Germany, or scholarship confirmation)
Proof of health insurance valid for the entire duration of stay in Germany (initially Schengen travel insurance, then private student health insurance upon arrival)
Proof of accommodation in Germany (e.g., rental contract, hotel booking, student housing confirmation)
Motivation letter explaining reasons for learning German and future plans
Curriculum Vitae (CV)
Academic or professional certificates (if available)
Proof of payment for the language course (if requested by embassy)
application_process_steps: Choose a recognized intensive German language school and enroll to obtain an acceptance letter.
Gather all required documents, including proof of financial means (e.g., open a blocked account).
Complete the visa application form and schedule an appointment at the German embassy or consulate in your home country.
Attend the visa interview, submit the complete application package, and pay the visa fee.
Wait for the visa application to be processed (typically 4-12 weeks, but can take up to 3 months).

Upon visa approval, receive your visa and travel to Germany. Within two weeks of arrival, register your address at the local residents' registration office (Anmeldung) and apply for a residence permit at the local Foreigners' Office (Ausländerbehörde) before your initial entry visa expires.

visas.name: Preparatory Course Visa
visas.description: This visa is for international students who need to undertake preparatory measures before commencing a full university degree in Germany. It primarily covers intensive German language courses required for university admission, attendance at a preparatory college (Studienkolleg), or comparable educational institutions, and compulsory internships related to studies.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are foreign students who have either been admitted to a German university (possibly with a preparatory language course requirement) or accepted by a preparatory college, or whose foreign school-leaving certificate is not directly recognized for German university entry and thus requires preparatory studies.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After successfully completing preparatory studies and a degree at a German university, visa holders can apply for an 18-month Job Seeker's Visa. During this period, they can search for qualified employment. Once employed, they can apply for a work permit or an EU Blue Card, which can lead to permanent residency (Settlement Permit) after typically 2 years of full-time employment with B1 German language skills, or longer without.
visas.renewal_conditions: The initial visa is typically for entry (e.g., 3 months) and must be converted to a residence permit in Germany. A residence permit for study preparation can be issued for a maximum of 2 years. For attending a preparatory language course, it is for a maximum of 18 months, and for attending a preparatory college, for a maximum of 1 year. An extension beyond these maximums for the *same purpose* is generally not possible. Extensions for study purposes (after preparatory courses leading to university admission) are typically for a further two years.
visas.tax_implications: Standard resident income tax rules apply. International students can work up to 140 full days or 280 half days per year. If income is below €450-€520 per month, taxes may not be required; otherwise, income tax deductions will apply, and a tax number will be issued.
benefits: Allows entry and residence in Germany for essential academic preparation, such as language acquisition or Studienkolleg.
Provides a clear pathway to transition to a full student visa upon successful completion of preparatory courses.
Permits part-time work up to 120 full days or 240 half days per year, offering financial flexibility (with conditions).
Offers a potential path to permanent residency in Germany after completing studies and gaining qualified employment.
required_documents: Fully completed and signed national visa application form (VIDEX).
Recent biometric passport photos (3.5 x 4.5 cm with a light background).
Valid passport (signed, valid for at least one year from visa issuance, with at least two blank pages).
Proof of residence (e.g., utility bill, rent contract in your home country).
Proof of language proficiency (e.g., B2 for studies, or specific level for preparatory course, issued by an ALTE-certified institution).
Curriculum Vitae (CV) in English or German, preferably Europass format.
Proof of sufficient means of subsistence (blocked account with €11,904 for one year, scholarship, or Declaration of Commitment).
Letter of acceptance/admission to a preparatory college (Studienkolleg) or a preparatory language course (intensive, at least 18 hours per week).
Academic qualifications/school-leaving certificates and transcripts.
Letter of motivation explaining the purpose of the course and future plans.
Proof of health insurance coverage (for initial entry and subsequent stay in Germany).
application_process_steps: Complete the online application form (VIDEX) via the Consular Services Portal and upload all required documents.
Submit your application online for a pre-check of completeness.
Book an appointment online at your diplomatic mission abroad (embassy/consulate) after documents have been pre-checked.
Attend the appointment, provide biometric data (fingerprints), submit original documents, and pay the visa fee.
Track your application status online.
Upon approval, the visa is issued for entry; apply for a residence permit at the local Foreigners' Office within two weeks of arrival in Germany.

visas.name: Family Reunification Visa
visas.description: The Family Reunification Visa (National D visa) in Germany allows non-EU citizens to join close family members who are either German citizens or legally residing in Germany with a valid residence permit. This visa provides a pathway for long-term stay, enabling family members to live together in Germany and eventually apply for a residence permit.
visas.target_applicant: Non-EU citizens who wish to permanently live in Germany with their spouse, registered civil partner, or minor children (under 18), or in some cases parents, who are German citizens or hold a valid German residence permit.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After several years of continuous legal residence in Germany (typically 5 years, or 3 years if the reference partner has a settlement permit or EU long-term residence permit), holders of the residence permit can apply for a permanent settlement permit. Under certain conditions, they may also apply for naturalization (German citizenship) if the reference partner obtains German citizenship.
visas.renewal_conditions: Must maintain eligibility criteria, including sufficient financial means and accommodation. For spouses, the residence permit in the first 3 years may depend on the continuation of the marriage or civil partnership.
benefits: Legal pathway to reside long-term in Germany with family.
Opportunity to work and study in Germany upon obtaining a residence permit.
Counts towards eligibility for permanent residency and German citizenship.
Access to public services, healthcare, and Germany's education system.
required_documents: Completed and signed national visa application form.
Valid passport (original + copies, issued within the last 10 years, valid for at least another 6-12 months, with at least 2 blank pages).
Two recent biometric passport photos.
Legalized or apostilled marriage certificate (for spouses/civil partners, translated into German).
Legalized or apostilled birth certificate (for children, translated into German).
German language certificate (A1 level for spouses, C1 for children over 16, with exemptions).
Copy of the sponsor's German passport, identity card, or certificate of naturalization (if German citizen).
Copy of the sponsor's valid residence permit (if foreign resident in Germany).
Copy of the sponsor's employment contract in Germany.
Copy of the sponsor's latest three payslips.
Copy of the sponsor's rental agreement proving adequate living space.
Copy of the sponsor's registration certificate (Meldebescheinigung).
Proof of adequate health insurance coverage (travel health insurance for initial visa validity, comprehensive for residence permit).
Proof of sufficient financial means of the sponsor to support the family without relying on public funds.
Consent of the other parent (if a child is joining a single parent).
Declaration of accuracy of information.
application_process_steps: Confirm eligibility for both the sponsor in Germany and the family member(s) applying.
Gather all required documents, ensuring they are legalized/apostilled and translated into German where necessary.
Fill out the national visa application form (available online via the Consular Services Portal or as a paper form).
Schedule a personal appointment at the German embassy or consulate in the applicant's country of residence.
Attend the appointment, submit the complete application package, provide biometric data (fingerprints and photo), and pay the visa fee.
After arrival in Germany, register the address at the local registration office (Bürgeramt) within two weeks.
Apply for a residence permit at the local Foreigners' Office (Ausländerbehörde) before the initial entry visa expires.

visas.name: Residence Permit for Financially Independent Persons (§7 Abs. 1 S. 3 AufenthG)
visas.description: This residence permit is for individuals who wish to reside in Germany without engaging in gainful employment, demonstrating sufficient personal income and/or assets to cover their living expenses. It falls under a discretionary clause of German immigration law for purposes not explicitly regulated elsewhere.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are financially independent individuals, such as retirees, who have substantial passive income or assets and do not intend to work in Germany.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After 5 years of continuous legal residence in Germany, applicants may apply for a permanent settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis). Requirements include demonstrating continued financial self-sufficiency, adequate health insurance, basic German language proficiency (B1 level), and no criminal convictions. German citizenship can typically be applied for after 5 years of legal residence, also requiring B1 German language skills.
visas.renewal_conditions: Must continue to demonstrate sufficient financial means to cover living expenses without relying on public funds, maintain adequate health insurance, and meet general requirements for a residence permit.
visas.tax_implications: If residing in Germany for more than 183 days per year, individuals are typically considered tax residents and are subject to German income tax on their worldwide income. Standard resident tax rules apply, with income tax rates ranging from 0% to 45%.
benefits: Right to reside in Germany.
Visa-free travel within the Schengen Zone.
Access to the German education system for accompanying children.
Potential path to permanent residency and citizenship.
required_documents: Valid passport
Completed application form
Biometric photographs
Proof of sufficient financial means (e.g., bank statements, evidence of assets, pension entitlements, rental income, dividends, royalties)
Proof of adequate health insurance coverage valid in Germany
Detailed explanation of the purpose and intended duration of stay, including the city of residence
Proof of accommodation in Germany (e.g., rental agreement)
No grounds for expulsion, such as criminal convictions or threats to public security
application_process_steps: Apply for a national D visa at the German embassy or consulate in your country of origin or permanent residence (unless you are a citizen of a visa-exempt country like Australia, Canada, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, the UK, or the USA, who can apply directly in Germany).
Gather all required documents, ensuring they are complete and, if necessary, officially translated into German.
Enter Germany with the national visa or as a visa-exempt national.
Register your address (Wohnsitzanmeldung) with the local registration office (Bürgerbüro) within 14 days of arrival.
Schedule an appointment with the local Foreigners' Authority (Ausländerbehörde) in your city of residence.
Submit your residence permit application and attend the appointment with all original documents and copies.

visas.name: Research Visa
visas.description: The Research Visa (also known as Guest Scientist Visa) is for non-EU/EEA/Swiss citizens who intend to reside in Germany for at least three months to conduct research at a recognized German research institution. It allows the holder to work at the specified research institute and also undertake teaching activities.
visas.target_applicant: Ideal applicants are researchers with a doctoral degree or a university degree that allows access to doctoral programs, who have been selected by a German research organization and have a signed hosting agreement or employment contract.
visas.path_to_residency_description: After successfully completing research activity, the residence permit may be extended for up to 18 months to seek alternative gainful employment. Researchers can apply for a settlement permit (permanent residency) in Germany after four years, provided they meet the general requirements for a settlement permit.
visas.renewal_conditions: The residence permit can be extended provided the applicant continues to fulfil the initial requirements, such as maintaining the hosting agreement or employment contract with a research institution.
benefits: Permission to work at the research institute listed in the contract.
Ability to take on teaching positions.
Mobility arrangements for conducting research in other EU states for a limited period.
Possibility to extend the residence permit.
Path to a settlement permit (permanent residency) after four years.
required_documents: Fully completed and signed national visa application form (e.g., VIDEX)
Current biometric passport photo (3.5 x 4.5 cm with light-coloured background)
Valid passport (personally signed, with at least two empty pages, valid for at least 3 months beyond intended stay, issued within the last 10 years)
Copy of passport biographic page and all non-empty pages
Hosting agreement ('Aufnahmevereinbarung') or relevant employment contract with a German research institute, signed by both parties
Proof of qualifications (e.g., doctoral degree, or university degree allowing access to doctorate programs, including transcripts if the degree doesn't state courses)
Proof of adequate financial means (e.g., through the hosting agreement/contract, or a blocked bank account showing at least 1,091 EUR per month for the duration of stay)
Proof of adequate travel health insurance for the entry period (and later full health insurance for the duration of stay in Germany)
Proof of accommodation for the intended duration of stay

If the research institution is not primarily public-funded and not listed by the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF): A declaration of assumption of costs related to the stay of the researcher
application_process_steps: Secure a hosting agreement or employment contract with a German research institution.
Gather all required supporting documents, including proof of financial means and adequate health insurance.
Complete the online national visa application form (VIDEX) and print it.
Book an appointment at the competent German Embassy or Consulate General in your country of residence (or through their external service provider like TLScontact).
Submit the application in person with all original documents and two sets of copies at the scheduled appointment.
Pay the application fee during the appointment.
Once the visa is issued, enter Germany and register your address (Melde-Bestätigung) with the local authorities within two weeks.
Apply for the full residence permit for research purposes at the local Foreigner's Office (Ausländerbehörde) in Germany after arrival.

Citizenship by Descent.desc: German citizenship is primarily based on the principle of *ius sanguinis* (descent). A child automatically acquires German citizenship at birth if at least one parent was a German citizen at that time, regardless of the child's place of birth. This is the most straightforward route for individuals born after January 1, 1975, to married German parents. Eligibility extends to complex historical situations, including descendants of those who lost German citizenship due to Nazi persecution between 1933-1945, with no statute of limitations or generational limit. Amendments in 2021 also allow for restoration of citizenship for those denied or forced to give it up due to previous gender-discriminatory regulations (e.g., born before 1975 to a German mother and foreign father). Since June 2024, dual citizenship is fully permitted when acquiring German citizenship by descent.

Naturalization.desc: As of 2026, the standard route for naturalization requires a minimum of five years of lawful residence in Germany, replacing a previous three-year fast-track option. Applicants must demonstrate sufficient German language skills (generally B1 level) and pass a naturalization test on the German legal system, society, and living conditions. Other key requirements include proof of identity and nationality, financial self-sufficiency without reliance on public benefits, a commitment to democratic values, and no serious criminal record. Dual citizenship is now generally permitted for naturalized citizens. Providing false or incomplete information intentionally during the application process can lead to a 10-year exclusion from naturalization.

Birthright.desc: German citizenship is not typically acquired solely by birth on German soil (pure *jus soli*) for children of non-German parents. Instead, it operates on the principle of *ius sanguinis*, where citizenship is conferred by descent from a German parent, regardless of the child's birthplace. If one parent is a German citizen at the time of birth, the child automatically acquires German citizenship.

Spouse and Family.desc: The new citizenship law, effective as of 2026, includes special routes for marriage-based citizenship. While the general naturalization period is five years, a shorter path of three years is available for spouses of German citizens, provided specific conditions are met. These conditions generally reinforce the link between naturalization and sustainable integration, including sufficient German language skills and financial independence.

tax_advice:
- **Personal Income Tax:** Germany operates a progressive income tax system (Einkommensteuer) with rates ranging from 0% to 45%. For 2026, the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag) is €12,348. Residents pay tax on their worldwide income, while non-residents are taxed only on German-source earnings.
- **Social Security Contributions:** Salaried workers make mandatory social security contributions, typically around 20% of their gross salary, covering public health, long-term care, pension, and unemployment insurance. Employers pay a similar amount.
- **Solidarity Surcharge (Solidaritätszuschlag):** A 5.5% surcharge on income tax, largely abolished for approximately 90% of taxpayers since 2021. For 2026, single filers only pay it if their annual income tax bill exceeds €20,350.
- **Church Tax (Kirchensteuer):** Members of officially recognized churches pay an additional surcharge of 8% or 9% of their income tax, depending on the federal state of residence.
- **Corporate Tax:** Companies based in Germany pay a federal corporate income tax (Körperschaftsteuer) at a flat rate of 15%, plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge, resulting in a total of 15.825%. Additionally, a municipal trade tax (Gewerbesteuer) varies by municipality, averaging around 14%, leading to a combined effective corporate tax rate of approximately 30%.
- **Value Added Tax (VAT):** The standard VAT rate (Umsatzsteuer) is 19%. A reduced rate of 7% applies to certain goods and services like selected food products, books, and public transport. From January 1, 2026, the VAT rate for restaurant and catering services (excluding beverages) will be permanently reduced to 7%. A 0% rate applies to exports and certain photovoltaic installations.
- **Capital Gains Tax:** Capital gains from financial investments are generally subject to a flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25%, plus the 5.5% solidarity surcharge, for an effective rate of 26.375%. Capital gains from the sale of private real estate held for 10 years or less are taxed at the individual's marginal income tax rate.
- **Double Taxation Treaties:** Germany has tax treaties with over 90 countries to prevent double taxation for residents.
local_tips:
- **Cost of Living:** The average cost of living for a single person is around €1,800-€2,500 per month, excluding rent. Munich, Frankfurt, and Hamburg are among the most expensive cities, while Leipzig, Dresden, and Dortmund offer lower costs. Rent is often the largest expense, significantly higher in major cities. Utilities for an 85m² apartment average around €302 per month.
- **Language:** While many Germans speak English, learning German is highly recommended for daily life, social integration, and professional opportunities. Many employers and institutions offer language courses.
- **Safety:** Germany is generally considered a safe country with low crime rates.
- **Bureaucracy and Registration:** Be prepared for extensive paperwork and potentially lengthy administrative processes, such as registering your address (Anmeldung) and setting up utilities. Patience and organization are key; German-speaking assistance can be very helpful. Expect things to take time and not all services to be digitalized.
- **Work-Life Balance:** Germany emphasizes a strong work-life balance, offering good vacation days and respecting working hours. Shops may close earlier than expected, and many are closed on Sundays.
